title: The foreigner's prayer (1 Kings 8:41–43)
hookLine: Solomon asks that a stranger's prayer in the Temple be heard too

lines: A LONG ROAD TO GET HERE.
cards: Somebody arrives from far away. Different clothes, a different accent, maybe a different language. They've heard about this place and walked a long road to reach it.
Now they stand in the courtyard among people who know the customs, and they don't. They pray anyway. Who is that prayer for?
Will anyone listen? Solomon's dedication prayer, in the middle of asking for his own people, stops to answer exactly that.

teach.b: Solomon has prayed for Israel in defeat, in drought, in famine and plague.

Then he turns to the foreigner, in Hebrew the nochri, who is not of Israel but comes out of a far country for the sake of God's name, having heard, the text says, of God's great name, strong hand and outstretched arm.

teach.h: DO ALL THAT THE STRANGER ASKS.
teach.b: When this stranger prays toward this house, Solomon asks, hear in heaven, and do according to all that the stranger calls to you for, so that all the peoples of the earth may know God's name.

Later readers noticed a detail. For Israel, Solomon asks God to give each person according to their ways, since God knows the heart. For the foreigner, he asks God to do according to all they call for.

teach.h: RASHI: SO NO ONE GOES HOME UNHEARD.
teach.b: The commentator Rashi reads that difference as care. Someone of Israel knows the relationship and can bear an answer of no.
But a foreigner who is turned away might say, I came all this way to that house, and I wasn't heard. So, Rashi says, Solomon asked that the stranger be answered in full.

teach.h: A HOUSE OF PRAYER FOR ALL PEOPLES.
teach.b: Later, the prophet Isaiah speaks of God's house as a house of prayer for all peoples. And the Torah tells Israel to care for the stranger, because they were strangers in the land of Egypt.
The house is built by one people, and it is open to another's voice.

how: Jews read Solomon's prayer for the foreigner in the book of Kings alongside the Torah's command to care for the stranger, and commentators such as Rashi ask why the foreigner's prayer is to be answered in full.

o: a foreigner: someone not of Israel, from far away
a priest who serves at the Temple's altar
a neighbor from another tribe of Israel

games.q: hear the stranger too — tap the pairs.
p: all that the stranger calls for
what Solomon asks God to do
a house of prayer for all peoples

s: Solomon's prayer is only for his own people
he stops to pray for the foreigner who comes out of a far country.
the stranger comes having heard of God's strong hand and outstretched arm
that's why, the text says, they come.
Rashi says the stranger should receive less than Israel
he reads it the other way: the stranger is answered in full, so no one goes home unheard.

games.q: you're dedicating your people's holy house. someday a foreigner may come to pray there. what do you ask?
o: that only your own people be heard here.
that the foreigner's prayer be heard in full.
that the foreigner first become one of your people.
games.why: Solomon asked God to do according to all that the stranger calls for, so that all the peoples of the earth may know God's name.

practice: Hold in mind someone you don't know, a person you passed on the street, a new family down the block, someone far from home whose story you heard, and wonder what they might be asking for tonight: safety, work, a place to belong.
If you pray, you can ask, in Solomon's spirit, that their prayer be heard; if you don't, just wish them well, plainly.

wordCard.voice: Nochri. The Hebrew word for a foreigner, the stranger from a far country Solomon asked God to hear fully. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a foreigner, someone from another land. the nochri of Solomon's prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: hear the stranger too. In Rashi's reading, the stranger shouldn't go home unheard. Until tomorrow.
